stories.headline: Update: Supertanker Hits Mine in Strait of Hormuz as Trump Says Iran Wants to Talk
stories.summary:
A supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil caught fire Friday after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said, according to state media. It was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion on Friday after using what the Guard described as unauthorized routes through the strait, according to The Associated Press.

Tehran has repeatedly said vessels must receive permission before traveling through the waterway. Iran warned last month that ships transiting without approval risked "destruction." The incidents add to pressure on global oil shipping at one of the world's most important energy chokepoints.

President Donald Trump said Iran wants to talk and predicted the conflict will end "very soon," according to Fox News Digital's live coverage. The remarks come as Qatar-led mediators work to restart US-Iran talks and as Iran's supreme leader has ordered a "maximum" response to any renewed US or Israeli attack. Iran's account of the tanker blasts comes from state media and has not been independently verified.

The story is being covered by 22 outlets across the political spectrum. What happens next depends on whether diplomacy gains traction and whether further commercial vessels are struck in the strait.

stories.headline: More Than 5,000 Dead in DR Congo's Deadliest Ebola Outbreak
stories.summary:
More than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to government data. Eight of the country's 26 provinces are affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases and a case fatality rate of 48.6%.

The outbreak began in May and became the country's deadliest in August, surpassing the 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018 and 2020. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history and the second largest ever recorded, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic that killed more than 11,325 people. The UN warns the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate."

The epicentre remains Ituri province, a conflict zone that complicates containment. The Bundibugyo species is responsible, and no approved treatment or vaccine exists for this strain, though clinical trials of vaccines are under way. Cases have been confirmed in Kenya (nine cases, two deaths), Nigeria and Uganda; Nigeria's disease control centre said two suspected cases were isolated on Saturday.

Health workers have been targeted. A nurse was killed earlier this week after local youths accused responders of contaminating water, a politician was beaten to death last month, and the Red Cross reported attacks on volunteers in August. The WHO's Africa office has called for expanded control measures, greater access to affected areas and community outreach.

stories.headline: US Embassy Warns of Credible Mass Casualty Threat at Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum
stories.summary:
The US embassy in Moscow said it was aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event on Saturday at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in the Russian capital. The embassy said it was coordinating with Russian authorities on a response.

The embassy urged people to avoid the area. Tsaritsyno is a large museum and park complex in southern Moscow that draws many visitors, particularly on weekends.

The warning provided no details on the nature or source of the threat, and Russian authorities had not been quoted in the initial reports from Bloomberg and Fox News. The alert is notable given that Washington and Moscow have limited diplomatic contact, and it follows heightened tensions tied to the war in Ukraine. Further information is expected as the situation develops.

stories.headline: Thai Court Adds Sentence to Rights Lawyer Arnon Nampa, Bringing Total to More Than 34 Years
stories.summary:
A Bangkok court on Friday sentenced human rights lawyer Arnon Nampa, 42, to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lese majeste law, Article 112. His offence was calling for the monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in 2020, at which he was dressed as the wizard.

This is one of 14 cases brought against him under the same charge, and his cumulative sentence now exceeds 34 years. Verdicts in two further cases are pending. "To me, this isn't a surprise," he told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."

The law carries three to 15 years for defaming, insulting or threatening the king, queen, heir-apparent or regent, and has been interpreted far more broadly, with prosecutions over comments about long-dead kings and even the king's dog. Since the 2020 student protests, 294 people, including 20 minors, have been prosecuted, receiving sentences of up to 50 years. Most are denied bail.

Thai officials defend the law as reflecting the country's culture and history, in which the monarchy is a revered pillar of society. Rights groups say it stifles public debate.

stories.headline: Update: Iran's Supreme Leader Orders 'Maximum' Response to Any Renewed US or Israeli Attack
stories.summary:
Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei told the country's top three military commanders that any renewed attack by the United States and Israel "must be met with an immediate and effective response, without geographical limitations," according to a statement from his office. He said the aim was to achieve "maximum deterrence." The statement described the order as part of preparations for a renewed confrontation and an effort to expand Tehran's options for retaliation.

Axios reported that this is the first publicly disclosed meeting between Khamenei and all the top commanders of Iran's armed forces since the war began. The meeting comes as President Trump is reported to be weighing major strikes against Iran.

Trump separately predicted that the war with Iran is "going to end soon," without offering details. Qatari mediators are pushing for a deal to restart US-Iran talks and avert renewed fighting after the midterm elections. The coming days are expected to show whether diplomacy or military escalation prevails, with both Washington and Tehran signaling readiness for either path.

stories.headline: Update: Evacuees From Russia-Occupied Oleshky Arrive in Ukraine After Local Ceasefire
stories.summary:
People evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky have crossed into Ukraine's Chernihiv region, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on X. Residents had been trapped without food, water and electricity, and many resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive. Zelensky thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts in brokering the local ceasefire that made the evacuation possible.

The evacuees left Oleshky on Friday in a convoy of 25 buses with space for 750 people, plus ambulances for those with limited mobility. They traveled through Russian-held territory to the southern Russian city of Anapa, flew to Gomel in Belarus, and were driven across Ukraine's northern border on Saturday. Several hundred people chose to stay despite the devastation. Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said they would still receive humanitarian assistance.

A humanitarian ceasefire took effect across the Kherson front on Tuesday, the first days of peace there in four years. It allowed the road out of the city to be cleared of mines and aid to be delivered, and it remains in place until the end of Sunday, November 1. Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova traveled to Oleshky together, making Lubinets the first Ukrainian official to visit Russian-occupied areas since the war began. Before the invasion, Oleshky had about 24,000 residents.

stories.headline: Update: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal President Suspended as Police Secure Court; President Nawrocki Cuts Trip Short
stories.summary:
Polish President Karol Nawrocki turned his plane around while en route to Senegal and returned home after police entered the Constitutional Tribunal, Poland's top court, and its president was suspended. "At such a moment, the President must be in Poland," Nawrocki wrote on X. The tribunal's website said president Bogdan Swieczkowski was suspended Friday.

Police said they secured the building after dozens of protesters gathered to oppose what they called the wrongful suspension, and that dangerous objects were thrown at officers. Some protesters prayed, while others carried signs attacking Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government.

Tusk, who returned to power in 2023 promising to restore judicial independence, defended the move. "Restoring the rule of law is our duty," he wrote, calling the process difficult but necessary after years of lawlessness under the previous government. Critics of the former Law and Justice (PiS) government accuse it of imposing political control over key courts, which led the EU to impose fines. Nawrocki, a PiS ally, has refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, and Swieczkowski, a PiS-era appointee, blocked judges chosen by the current majority from taking up their duties. Tusk's efforts have been vetoed by two successive presidents aligned with PiS.

stories.headline: California Home Affordability Stuck at 19% as Buyers Need $228,000 Income
stories.summary:
Only 19% of California households could afford a median-priced existing single-family home in the third quarter, according to figures released Friday by the California Association of Realtors. The rate was unchanged from the previous quarter and from a year earlier. Even as prices dipped, higher mortgage rates kept the cost of buying high.

The minimum qualifying household income was $228,000, flat from the second quarter and $4,400 higher than a year earlier. The monthly payment, including principal, interest, taxes and insurance, was $5,700, more than twice the national average of $2,760. The required income has topped $200,000 in 15 of the past 16 quarters.

Regional figures were steeper. The Los Angeles metro median was $847,030, requiring $215,600 in income, while Los Angeles County's median was $958,450, requiring $244,000. In Orange County, the median was $1.47 million, requiring $374,400 in income. The association warned mortgage rates could remain elevated in coming months because inflation is likely to stay high in the near term, further limiting buyers' purchasing power.

stories.headline: Update: Spain Train Disaster Death Toll Reaches 69, Clouding Sánchez's Re-election Bid
stories.summary:
Rescuers have recovered 69 bodies from the wreckage of a high-speed train collision in Toledo, in central Spain, on the line south from Madrid. It is the second major crash on the corridor in nine months. In January, two trains collided near Cordoba and killed 46 people. The latest disaster comes weeks before a snap general election called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Transport Minister Oscar Puente has suggested human error was to blame since the first hours after the collision. On Friday he held a second press conference to set out what he called the "objective facts." He said Spain's LZB signalling safety system is neither old nor inadequate, and noted that Germany and Austria use the same technology. He said the system has failed 170 times so far this year, which he called normal and near the EU average. Control then shifts to manual operation, and Puente said a series of human errors proved catastrophic. A controller reportedly told a stalled train to restart, clearing it to travel at up to 160 km/h even though a second train was stuck ahead. Audio calls and screens in the Madrid control centre showed the impending collision, but the advancing train was never ordered to stop.

The opposition People's Party and others have called for Puente's resignation as a moral and ethical step. He has refused, calling it his duty to remain and to work to restore confidence in rail travel. The formal investigation has only just begun, and a probe into the January Adamuz crash remains open, with initial reports pointing to a crack in the rails. Pollster Paco Camas of Ipsos noted that this is a serious accident and the second in a very short time, and Spaniards will take a lot of persuading.

stories.headline: Final Midterm Weekend: Michigan Senate Democrats Feud, Ohio Governor Race Tightens
stories.summary:
With four days until the Nov. 3 midterm elections, campaigns are in their final push and several key races are showing strain. In Michigan, Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's campaign told former primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens to stay away from his events, according to Politico and a source who confirmed it to Fox News. Stevens has sharply criticized El-Sayed's views on Israel, and her fiancé has publicly endorsed Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed's opponent. The dispute casts doubt on a planned Sunday appearance with Rep. Jim Clyburn meant to show party unity.

Republicans have made El-Sayed's faith and associations a central line of attack. At a Rogers event, Sen. Ted Cruz called him "a theocratic zealot" and "jihadist leprechaun" and argued he would endanger service members by sharing secrets with terrorist groups. Cruz and other Republicans have sought to link El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, which he has condemned. If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim U.S. senator.

In Ohio, a Republican-funded private poll reportedly showed Vivek Ramaswamy trailing Democrat Amy Acton by 8 points for governor, a 6-point drop from an earlier survey, after a Ramaswamy ad featured Acton's estranged mother. Democrats call the ad a galvanizing moment. In Georgia, the governor's race between Keisha Lance Bottoms and Rick Jackson remains tight, while Sen. Jon Ossoff leads Rep. Mike Collins by a sizable margin in polls. NBC reports that Trump has avoided New Hampshire, a state he lost three times, while campaigning in other tight Senate races.

stories.headline: Update: Netanyahu's Likud Alleges Arab Parties 'Stole' Election as Israel Heads Toward Impasse
stories.summary:
With more than 90 percent of ballots counted, Israel's election appears to have produced no clear winner despite the highest turnout in nearly three decades. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and its allies are on track for 53 seats, which leaves the governing coalition without a majority. Neither of the two main blocs appears to have enough seats to form a government without relying on Arab parties.

Likud has alleged foreign interference and claimed Arab-led parties "stole" the election after the coalition lost its majority. BBC analysts say all signs point to an impasse, and the most likely outcome may be new elections. The vote had been widely viewed as one of the most pivotal in the country's history, with security, democracy and ultra-Orthodox military conscription as central issues.

Arab Israeli turnout, often depressed by disaffection, was boosted this time by a strong push to remove the right-wing coalition. Coalition talks are expected to be difficult, and the fraud allegations are likely to sharpen tensions as the final count is certified.

stories.headline: Trump Tariffs Idle Paper Mill, Threatening Quebec Town of Témiscaming
stories.summary:
The Témiscaming paper mill in Quebec has been idle since early October, when American owner RYAM began an "economic shutdown" for an indefinite period after US-Canada trade talks broke down and President Trump imposed additional tariffs. Most of the mill's 360 employees are out of work and are kept afloat with partial pay from government tariff relief. Property values in the town have fallen almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs line the streets.

Residents fear essential workers, from grocery clerks to hospital doctors, could leave. Local contractors have already laid off staff, and union leader Stéphane Lefebvre said a 10 percent job loss in a major city would dominate the news. Canada's national unemployment rate has held steady near 6.5 percent with tepid growth, but industries hit by tariffs of up to 50 percent, including steel, aluminium, autos and lumber, face deep pain.

The situation raises questions about whether Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is doing enough while a trade deal remains elusive. The White House has lifted tariffs on some Canadian goods as the midterms near, but the mill remains closed. The town last faced an existential threat in 1973, when a previous American owner threatened to close the mill.
